issues.title: Reposition away from "profile of AIMS" to only having "relationship to AIMS", and revisit Table of Contents
issues.author: pcarleton
issues.body:
This draft does fit the conceptual model put forward in [AIMS](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-klrc-aiagent-auth/), however calling it a "profile" doesn't quite fit.

This issue is to track revising the draft to be less dependent on AIMS, so it needs:
* to remove "profile" language
* to revisit the concepts section to be able to stand by itself more readily

Once this issue is complete, the following should be true:
* A reader does not need to read all of AIMS to make use of this draft
* A reader familiar with AIMS should know how this draft lines up with its conceptual model of agents as workloads

comments.author: PieterKas
comments.body:
Nice! Great to see the Privacy Considerations in there :)

Building on the above,  maybe we can: 

1. Make the **Workload Authorization Grant** section more focused and constrain it to the Grant format and processing (including claims)
2. Move anything to do with the AS to an **Authorization Server Processing** to it's own section (allows us to focus changes for AS's in one place)
3. Break out **Trust Establishment** as its own section (we can set the context for why it is needed with a diagram under Concepts/Overview, along with a typical mermaid diagram showing the flows e2e)?

issues.title: Pick small set of standard claims
issues.author: pcarleton
issues.body:
We want:
* A small set of claims that are common among implementations (target: max of 3)
* extensibility to add more claims if a platform and resource want
* Clearly specify which claims can be trusted for policy decisions, and clarify that others cannot
* ability to re-use existing authz modeling where appropriate (i.e. I want this agent to have the same permissions as humans on this team)

The leading candidate is `roles`, `groups` and `entitlements` from https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7643#section-4.1.2 / https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9068#section-2.2.3.1

If that does end up being what we do, we need to:
* play out an example of the agent platform giving claims like roles / groups if they're not specific to the platform
* decide whether they need to be namespaced by FQDN (or if issuer namespacing is sufficient)
* explain relationship to #3

comments.author: PieterKas
comments.body:
It may be good to elaborate on the problem we are trying to solve by picking any additional claims beyond what is defined in RFC 7523 and/or ID-JAG? What is the specific use case?

My first instinct is that we should not make any claims beyond what is needed by RFC 7523 REQUIRED in this draft. That would maximise compatibility with existing infrastructure and minimise the assumptions about the deployment. What mandatory values would we need beyond what is described already?

For the examples of roles, groups and entitlements my concern would be that values for those claims are things that may have meaning on one platform, but once you cross a trust boundary, it may have different meaning in a different domain. It also assumes a certain kind of underlying RBAC system, which although common, may not be universal.

In terms of optional claims, the three claims you describe feel like something that falls under the ID-JAG "authorization_details" claim and can be described in a RAR object (which may still need to be defined, but perhaps that is something that gets profiled elsewhere?).

I am also curious about the choice of picking values from SCIM as claims - is there specific upside we expect from that (other than these values matching attributes provisioned for users through SICM)?

comments.author: pcarleton
comments.body:
Summary of a related discussion with @PieterKas and @arndt-s and where I'd like to take this issue:

**What the claims are for.** The motivating case is "this agent gets roughly my team's permissions". The mapping from platform-asserted claims to resource-side permissions is intended to be explicit and happen when the trust relationship is established (an admin maps the `team-foobar` group claim to the permissions already defined for team-foobar in the resource server); it is never implicit (the enterprise-IdP case in #3 may be the exception). A small set of common claim names makes that mapping UI consistent across agent platforms: pick "roles" from a list rather than type a key/value and hope there is no typo. None of these claims would be required.

**Why SCIM**: Underlying assumption: the permissions an agent needs in order to be useful look more like a user's than a service account's, hence leaning on SCIM's modeling (groups / roles / entitlements). Pieter's pushback: those names assume RBAC (there is a whole *-BAC universe), and ID-JAG puts this kind of information in `authorization_details` (RAR), and keeps it optional.

Options discussed:
1. Specify no claims.
2. Specify only that authorization-bearing information goes in `authorization_details`; everything else is informational (debug / audit helpers).
3. Recommend a few common optional claims (groups, roles, entitlements) with worked examples of how they map.
4. Full namespacing (URNs / issuer-qualified claim names). Nobody is pushing for this.

Agreement so far: (2) over (1), as long as it is optional. Open question from Pieter: is there an existing RAR type we could reuse rather than define one, and would MCP then use these values for a stronger conformance/interop requirement?

Arndt's point, which I agree with: resource servers need to know which claims can be relied on for authorization decisions — platform-controlled vs admin-controlled vs user-controlled. Without this, you can run into issues like with github actions where a resource assumes a platform is asserting something important in a claim (like repo name + branch), but in fact that claim is user-controlled, leading to accidentally performing actions that were meant to only happen off of the main branch of a repo.

Two shapes were floated: a verified / non-verified split of claim sets (the OSW idea), or a flat rule that every claim in the assertion MUST be asserted by the issuer (simpler, harder to enforce and platforms have incentives to let customers inject claims). `authorization_details` is itself a clear "this is auth-bearing" marker, which is part of the appeal of (2).

Proposed direction for -01:
- Normative floor = (2): authorization-bearing information, if present, goes in `authorization_details` (RFC 9396); the grant itself carries no scope unless the token request asks for one (RFC 7523 §2.1).
- A short RECOMMENDED, optional claim set per (3), each with a worked example of the explicit mapping step.
- Text distinguishing platform-asserted claims from customer-injected ones, so a Resource AS never treats an unverified claim as auth-bearing by accident.
- Nothing in (4)

In general, this spec is aiming to be the minimum viable spec for this step of the exchange, so all of these we'll want to be optional.

comments.author: bc-pi
comments.body:
I'm struggling to see/understand how `authorization_details` would work here and the claims* about what that claim does in ID-JAG. 

\* pun intended

comments.author: bc-pi
comments.body:
One (other?) potential problem with the claims from SCIM is that they aren't defined very well despite being registered

https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9068#name-registry-content-2

https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/jwt-reg-review/sokgjH43qzp9nK5iq-Qo4J8QFRY/ 

https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/oauth/iJFODO2hW6rTlVV3pnJKxyRMQMU/

comments.author: pcarleton
comments.body:
I'm tempted to leave `authorization_details` fairly unspecified in order to leave room for things like payments if folks want to use it for that in the future, e.g. what's layed out here: https://yaron-zehavi.github.io/oauth-rich-authorization-requests-metadata/draft-ietf-oauth-rar-metadata-remediation-00/draft-ietf-oauth-rar-metadata-remediation.html#name-authorization-server-metada

regarding the SCIM claims, I was thinking just plain strings to start. In the "direct" deployment model (Platform -> Service provider, no IdP involved), it is most convenient to just use strings, and not try to teach the platform the full SCIM schema.  The purpose of using `groups` in the direct model is only as a familiar way to convey properties between the platform and service provider.  There will need to be a "mapping" step, where the Service Provider lets the admin decide what access the WAG grants in the platform based on properties.  The main / only benefit of mentioning the SCIM claim set here is to give a small nudge to make that "mapping" step a little less "wild west". (e.g. "platform_foo_team4=true" claim coming from Platform4 should map to this permission in Service6, vs. having some nicer UX around when you see "team4" in a `groups` claim.) 

related: I believe if we're making agent platforms full SCIM clients, that's likely not desirable, and instead would be better served by the "idp mediated" model (Platform -> IdP -> Service Provider) that we've started sketching out a little in #3 (and to re-iterate, I want to leave basically *all* "how does this work with an idp" specification out of this document, apart from nodding to it as a deployment model, and potentially stating that Service Providers should be able to be mostly agnostic of whether the token is coming from an IdP or from a platform)

comments.author: jiyun-ant
comments.body:
I'd like to get more clarity on emitting agent groups, here is where I'd land this section, building on the thread above:

- `groups` (and `roles`) are opaque strings, unique and stable within the issuing tenancy: within `iss`, or within (`iss`, `tenant`) on a shared issuer. The platform documents how they're formed. It can be computed (all agents in a tenancy, all agents in one chat app workspace) or admin-assigned groups.
- They are assertions, not permissions. The AS/RS maps (iss, tenant, value) to local teams or roles through a mapping the customer's admin sets up at trust establishment. No mapping, no access. Never merged with human groups that happen to share a name.
- If the relying party wants a directory object for sharing UIs or access reviews, that's the SCIM agent group (I-D.wzdk-scim-agent-resource) carrying the same id in `externalId`; the claim is then the per-request proof of membership.
- Request-specific authorization data stays in `authorization_details`, as discussed above.

Happy to send this as PR text with a worked example if it matches where everyone is.

issues.title: Discuss integration points with enterprise IdP (proposal: out of scope for this draft)
issues.author: pcarleton
issues.body:
This draft currently aims to be as simple as possible and targeted at an agent platform issuing its own tokens, similar to how a k8s cluster has an OIDC provider that's trusted in some WIF implementations today.

However, there is a deployment model that could make sense here where folks want their enterprise IdP to be the single source of truth into what has access into their system, e.g. to revoke an agent's access in the IdP instead of needing to go to the agent platform.

The rough shape that seems most promising here is:
* The agent platform is trusted by the IdP to create agent identities
* The resource authorization server trusts the IdP
* The IdP is responsible for ensuring groups / roles / entitlements align with the organization-wide authz model

This has a few implications:
* The agent platform needs to exchange its platform-issued token for one issued by the IdP
* The agent platform still provides the `client_assertion` to prove the request is coming from the platform
* the IdP *may* choose to do a SCIM operation or other lifecycle management into the resource authorization server if it needs to
  * this implies that the token exchange may need to be asynchronous if a stateful provisioning is happening
* the resource authorization server may want to rely on a stateful provisioning process
 
I'm proposing this IdP-integrated deployment model can be lightly mentioned in this draft, but the WAG draft keeps "how does the agent get its authorization grant" out of scope.  (i.e. an IdP-integrated deployment would be in a separate draft).

Also note, this deployment model looks very similar to ID-JAG's typical model, with a small variation: rather than an id_token issued by the IdP in its token exchange, the IdP would be accepting a token from the agent platform itself (likely a WAG).  This is also related to: https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant/issues/73

issues.title: Discuss: deployment model considerations for issuer count != 1
issues.author: jtrochet-openai
issues.body:
Hello,

I work at and make decisions for OpenAI in relation to the identity and authorization semantics of its internal platforms. I'm strongly aligned with the draft specification as-is, but I believe it's important for the standard to explicitly consider tenancies that accept multiple issuers and make recommendations for unambiguous behavior under those conditions.

For enterprises at medium to large scale, it's frequently the case for multiple compute environments to exist, each hosting its own credential issuer. Explicitly condoning multi-issuer configuration will allow enterprises of this scale to integrate with WAG-implementing service providers without the need to host specific infrastructure for credential fan-in.

Simultaneously, for relatively-small enterprises, the operational cost of reliably self-hosting a single issuer can be prohibitive. My expectation is that customers at this scale will host agentic workloads in cloud providers. Workload credentials issued by those cloud providers are already in common use through unstandardized federated credential flows, and their use for agentic workloads is a logical extension for these small enterprises. These small enterprises may have infrastructure spanning multiple cloud providers, each with their own issuer.

Both of these cases assume that WAG will be used with credentials issued to specific compute, rather than credentials issued by inference providers such as OpenAI itself. However, if industry practice converges on inference providers acting as the Agent Platform (and credential issuer), supporting multiple providers remains important by enabling the capability for enterprises to use different inference providers in different situations.

In sum, I believe that enterprise use cases across the spectrum of possible scales will be best-served by having the WAG standard explicitly contemplate multi-issuer use cases. I believe that the number of issuers that will be required by most use cases will remain small, however, and a mechanism for configuration beyond the Customer Administrator manually configuring each issuer in each tenancy does not need to be contemplated.

If multiple issuers are taken as a normal expectation, I recommend the specification explicitly describe best practices for avoiding inter-issuer subject namespace collisions. Here are some potential approaches, in my order of preference:

- Require the use of SPIFFE IDs as subject claims, with 1:1 trust-domain-to-issuer bindings a core part of the configuration made by Customer Administrators; this minimizes the footprint within the WAG specification by inheriting SPIFFE issuance/validity behavior
- Describe a mechanism to exclusively restrict the issuance of identities within different configured issuers, such that no two issuers may claim the same identity
- Synthetically convert unnamespaced subject identifiers from issuer claims to namespaced identifiers, such as SPIFFE IDs, based on the metadata of the configured issuer, during token exchange

comments.author: pcarleton
comments.body:
Hi @jtrochet-openai ! Thanks for reading the draft and taking the time to write this up. 

I very much agree we need to account for >1 issuers. My closest analogy for an "agent platform" is a single kubernetes cluster with it's own OIDC provider per-cluster.  In that mental model, it's very common to have multiple issuers coming into the same resource server.  If the draft makes any statements that contradict that as a possibility, let's definitely correct them. This has come up a few times, so I'm realizing I have not captured that mental model in the draft very well. We can tweak the intro and abstract to make it clearer this will be multiple issuers * multiple resources.

On the issue of `sub` overlap, I also agree with this, and came across it in my initial demo implementation (you can try it out here: https://wagd1-agent-platform.val.run/).  A naive implementation using JWT access tokens would just copy the `sub` over to the `access_token`, however the sub is only guaranteed to be unique inside 1 issuer.  I don't think we want to specify the shape of access tokens (one of the key principles here, borrowed from ID-JAG, is that the OAuth server should only need to change it's `/token` endpoint, not it's access token shape).  My current opinion is we should cover that in a security consideration (cc @arndt-s related to our previous discussion) 

On the proposed approaches:

1. I agree SPIFFE ID's are a good fit for `sub` here, but I don't want to require SPIFFE for this specification. I would rather we specify the requirements that we have and note that SPIFFE ID's satisfy them.  Part of the reason to keep this separate from ID-JAG was to have this spec be a small, relatively narrow and self-contained unit, and tying it into SPIFFE ID's or WIT means many more required concepts that you don't necessarily need.  Put another way: If you're already doing SPIFFE, great, you've got something that works.  If you're not already doing SPIFFE, I don't want to send you on a "go understand SPIFFE" quest in order to get this working.
2. Yes agree here, this is most similar to the security consideration, and I think is the bare minimum.
3. Similarly, I think this could go in the security consideration, because I don't want to require implementers to change their access tokens and downstream systems, but they do need to be aware of pitfalls.

comments.author: jtrochet-openai
comments.body:
I actually expect that most SP-side implementations won't take the naive "copy the subject over" approach—most SaaS providers I'm aware of have internal subject identifiers (bound to external subject/issuer at the edge and embedded in the application database) that they'll want to use. This binding is already necessary where multiple traditional human IdPs are in use. Rather than copy the `sub` over and force their application logic to learn what that means, I suspect they'll do some sort of provision-on-demand on first token issuance, and issue tokens with the internal identifier.

This means some nice things for SPIFFE—if we require SPIFFE here, then services that exchange for an internal subject will, as they do for current external subject IDs, bind the opaque SPIFFE to that subject, with only the token exchange layer needing to be aware of SPIFFE semantics. For the rare SPs that do propagate external subject IDs inward, they will already need to support relatively generic opaque subject structures, so no new SPIFFE logic is necessary inside the application. In both cases, the AS essentially encapsulates the SPIFFE-trust domain validation logic, which provides an internal guarantee of subject ID uniqueness across per-tenant configured issuers.

Personally, I increasingly believe the concepts that SPIFFE IDs encode to be part of the essential complexity of cross-issuer identity verification: if we don't incorporate them via SPIFFE (not necessarily traditional SVIDs, to be clear), then we'll still need to bring them in via, as you mentioned, a "security consideration" note, and we'll be relying on "best practices" to ensure them, rather than pointing to a standard with clear correctness criteria. 

In other words, I see the "go understand SPIFFE" quest as being essential for someone setting up a multi-issuer architecture. If they already understand the fundamentals of why subject claims need namespacing, SPIFFE IDs will be immediately understandable. If they don't, the SPIFFE spec is instructive on why maintaining that namespacing is critical, and that instruction would need to happen anyway.

issues.title: Issuer per tenancy: MUST → SHOULD, with a standard `tenant` claim
issues.author: pcarleton
issues.body:
-00 (Trust Establishment) says a platform serving multiple customers MUST use a distinct issuer per tenancy, because the issuer is the boundary the AS allowlist expresses. Two things push against the MUST:

- A platform that already runs one issuer (one metadata document, one JWKS) would need per-tenant issuer URLs and metadata just for this grant,  the single largest piece of new surface the draft asks of a platform. (example issuers in this boat: )
- An AS that evaluates claims can pin (issuer, tenant) exactly as precisely as it can pin an issuer, so this allows for more flexibility.

Costs of allowing a `tenant` claim:
- If we allow it ever, then every consumer needs to process it always, and a missing tenant claim when one is needed becomes a failure mode we have to consider
- It's slightly more complicated for the admin flow to copy 2 values over (issuer + tenant claim), than just a single string (per-tenant-issuer)


I still thing distinct issuers is the better path for someone implementing from scratch, however, I think it's worth the flexibility / matches reality more closely to allow for the tenant claim.

Proposal for -01:
- Distinct issuer per tenancy becomes RECOMMENDED. A platform that shares an issuer across tenancies MUST include a `tenant` claim (single opaque, stable string) and the AS allowlist entry pins issuer + tenant.
- Issuer metadata MUST state which mode the issuer uses. (more discussion needed here, I want to prevent the missing claim when needed causing issues)

Related: #6 (subject namespace collisions at multi-issuer ASes).

comments.author: jtrochet-openai
comments.body:
An alternative to an explicit tenant claim would be to define a "claim-restricting" semantic on the issuer-tenancy binding. This would avoid encoding a specific structure for tenancy claims while allowing the Customer Administrator to make informed decisions on a per-issuer basis. You can see this architecture being used in OIDC federation between CI actions like Github workflows and cloud providers like AWS and Azure—the individual configuring the integration point is expected to understand the claims supported by that particular token issuer.

Service providers may end up creating "templates" for known, very popular multitenant issuers that exercise this vocabulary—for example, if a particular agentic platform is in common use, and is known to differentiate its tenancies by a particular claim, service providers could reasonably make "which tenancies do you trust?" part of their UI-based configuration for that particular issuer, rather than requiring Customer Administrators to configure the claim-restricting semantic exactly.

comments.author: arndt-s
comments.body:
One idea, similar to @jtrochet-openai's  I've floated around is to document "required" claims on the issuer metadata endpoint.

```
{
   "issuer": "https://agent-platform.acme.org",                         <-- GLOBAL issuer
   "jwks_uri": "https://agent-platform.acme.org/jwks.json",
   "required_assertion_claims": [
       "org_id"                       <-- not "tenant"
    ]
}
```

`required_assertion_claims` is a list of claims that are present in the assertion and MUST be checked.

If we want to support existing issuers we should also support those that don't have a `tenant` claim. For instance Entra with `tid` or Google Workspace with `hd`.

comments.author: pcarleton
comments.body:
I think where we're landing:
* we want to support IdP's that use a shared issuer
* a `tenant` claim is one option we can recommend, but can't require given the goal of supporting existing deployments that _don't_ use `tenant`
* we could also specify a metadata-based approach to explaining which claims define the notion of a `tenant` along with `issuer`.  (related from previous discussion: we could also use the metadata based approach for defining which claims are set by which authority, platform, admin or agent-author).
* the fallback we'd need likely in any case is "which claim is load-bearing is communicated out of band", e.g. for ones that don't use tenant, you have to figure it out per issuer (e.g. knowing that Entra uses `tid`).  I don't love that mechanism, but may just be required to note, e.g. have bullets (2) & (3) be SHOULD's.

@arndt-s  I think for (3), we'd want to specify that it is specifically for uniqueness, rather than just generically "required", right? e.g.  you might have a required "scope" claim, but that wouldn't be treated the same way

comments.author: arndt-s
comments.body: Agreed that the `required_assertion_claims` name is not ideal. Maybe we also just need to make it explicit and call it "required_tenant_claims". My thought was actually a bit further and use the same mechanics for claims that are not directly describing the tenant but within. As a concrete example, a Github organization is the tenant, but the repository is an essential thing to check. Or Kubernetes, where the namespace is a very common claim to check.

issues.title: agent accountability in downstream systems
issues.author: pcarleton
issues.body:
AS's accept an Agent on its first assertion, this leaves a question of: who in the authorization server's organization answers for an Agent, and how is that established without an administrator?

The point of the Agent acting as itself is that access survives org changes (the person who set it up leaves, nothing breaks). Tying it to one person brings that fragility back; not tying it to anyone leaves the resource side with a potential gap in terms of audit and compliance.

Some options to consider, although not clear they need to be specified in this document:
1. Implicit from a Platform claim (e.g. team → that team's responsible person).
2. Adoption on first use by any user. No access until a user takes it on. One extra interaction, still self-service; still has the hand-off problem when that user changes teams or leaves.
3. An owner claim from the Platform. Simple on the wire, but the value is from the Platform's domain and the authorization server likely can't map it to one of its users.

Does the document need more than the open issue here, and if so, mechanism (2/3) or guidance (1)?

pulls.title: Clarify property assertion and freshness semantics
pulls.author: FutureEnterprises
pulls.body:
Addresses the trust-boundary portion of #2.

This change separates three facts that the current text places close together:

- An Agent Property is an issuer assertion made when the grant is issued.
- `iat` and `exp` establish the grant's age and acceptance window, not whether mutable state is still true later.
- Roles, groups, entitlements, and similar values are interpreted through the Resource Server's issuer-scoped local mapping. They are not portable permission assignments.

If a policy requires a Property to remain true at presentation or access time, the deployment must obtain evidence current for that time. Otherwise, grant and access-token lifetimes bound the stale-claim exposure.

This does not choose the final property vocabulary, require a specific status mechanism, or add an EMILIA dependency.

Verification:

- `make` completed successfully.
- The existing EMILIA WAG-to-AEB composition fixture reproduced 15 of 15 checks against the pinned WAG-00 source.

comments.author: pcarleton
comments.body:
Merging, thanks for this note! The assertion-vs-freshness distinction and the issuer-scoped-mapping point are both right and I want to call them out in.

Two notes so nothing surprises you later: the properties text is being reworked under #2, so this may move; and I will likely soften the two "deployment MUST" sentences to SHOULD-level guidance in Security Considerations, since "the deployment" isn't a wire actor the AS or RS can check.

pulls.title: Aims reframe
pulls.author: pcarleton
pulls.body:
Closes #1.

the draft called itself a profile of draft-klrc-aiagent-auth (AIMS) but never
actually depended on it: every rule is stated in terms of RFC 7523, RFC
8414 metadata and published JWK Sets. This drops the profile framing so
an AS implementer can read this document alone.

- AIMS moves from normative to informative references; "profile" is
  removed throughout.
- "Relationship to AIMS" becomes an informative correspondence table
  (agent acting on its own behalf, AIMS 10.4.2) instead of inherited
  requirements.
- New Concepts > Overview: the parties, the three steps (trust
  establishment once, instantiation, per-request grant) and an
  end-to-end figure, so the document stands on its own.
- Abstract/Introduction wording: no administrator-performed
  per-workload registration step; drop the "self-contained" and "no
  per-workload credential" claims (the grant is per workload; we build
  on RFC 7523).
- Agent Identity Model: single-agent policy is an exact match on the
  sub value.
- Section anchors added ({#introduction}, {#conventions}, {#overview},
  {#aims}); decision log D13.

No change to the grant format, claims, or AS processing rules.

pulls.title: Property claims: platform plus platform-prefixed context claims in place of ctx
pulls.author: jiyun-ant
pulls.body:
Replaces the composite `ctx` Property in the example assertion and in the Properties section with flat collaboration-context claims: `platform`, naming the collaboration platform the Agent acts in (a chat or work application — not the Agent Platform), plus that platform's own workspace and channel identifiers under claim names prefixed with the platform name (`example_workspace_id`, `example_channel_id` for a platform named `example`). Records the choice as D15 in the decision log; O2 now points at it for registration.

Why: separate flat string claims can be matched directly by a Resource Server (cloud IAM trust-policy conditions included) without parsing a composite value, and the prefix keeps identifiers of different platforms apart. Which claims an issuer populates stays its choice.

Offered as input per CONTRIBUTING.md — happy to turn this into an issue, or to move D15 to Open, if you'd rather settle it in review.

pulls.title: draft-01: slim down
pulls.author: pcarleton
pulls.body:
Proposed -01 text, cut down to be only what's required for interop.

**Changed**

- `aud` is the authorization server's issuer identifier, a single value
- The Agent Identifier is an opaque string
- JWK can be manually entered
- "Platform" is one tenant; "Platform registration" is the authorization server's record of one trusted Platform. Under a shared issuer identifier the registration needs a claim that tells Platforms apart (`tenant` RECOMMENDED for new shared issuers). (Relates to #7)

**Small normative additions**

- `resource` REQUIRED
- optional `scope` claim as in ID-JAG
- no refresh tokens
- first-seen stated as "MUST NOT reject solely because the `sub` is unseen"
- error responses say who must act, using existing error codes;

**Cut**

- AIMS correspondence table (the Overview and figure stay, shortened)
- Scope section (now in the abstract)
- retirement prose (now the lifetime rule)
- the property vocabulary (points at the `roles`/`groups`/`entitlements` names already in use, defines none). Unused references removed.

**Added**
Security Considerations is a list for now; a fuller treatment is coming separately.

I could see this going one of two ways:
* deliberately emphasize ephemeral: that would simplify things. for example, the story around lifecycle would be much easier, and it would be clear that a human can't be in the loop to do any provisioning step.
* stick with "project-duration" / semi-durable agents as the canonical use case: makes the "how hands-free is it really?" question more up in the air (which means we have to emphasize the difference between admins and users), and also makes our "no lifecycle semantics defined" stance a bit weaker.

One middle ground could be to have the examples be around ephemeral, since it is the simplest version, and then have a section, maybe in deployment considerations, about "stateful principals" or something like that to call out that it's at least supported and what you want to consider if you're doing that. wdyt?

Platform: the party that instantiates and manages the lifecycle of workloads ("Agents").

pulls.title: Fix idnits findings from the -01 submission
pulls.author: pcarleton
pulls.body:
Addresses two of the three idnits findings on the -01 submission.

- `SUBMISSION_TYPE_UNEXPECTED`: removes `submissiontype: IETF` from the front matter. That key is the only thing that puts a `submissionType` attribute on the `rfc` element, and the datatracker has no stream for this individual draft.
- `REFERENCE_NOT_USED`: removes RFC 8628 from the informative references. The text never cites it.

Not fixed: `LINE_PI`. The `<?line N?>` processing instructions are emitted by kramdown-rfc itself (one per `---` section, plus one after the BCP 14 boilerplate) and there is no option to suppress them, so it would affect any draft built this way. It is a warning only.

Not verified locally: the fixes were reasoned from the submitted XML and the kramdown-rfc and xml2rfc sources, and I could not run a build here. The next submission's idnits result will confirm.
